notes: Overall a very clean, well-structured implementation. Architectural adherence is strong: services own their data exclusively, the event bus is properly used for inter-service communication (task.assigned, task.statusChanged, comment.added), and the Router is the sole HTTP entry point. The singleton eventBus export is a pragmatic in-memory pub/sub that satisfies the constraint. Completeness is high — all five services are implemented with full CRUD, forward-only status transitions work correctly, notifications are triggered by all three event types, and a thorough demo script exercises every endpoint. Minor completeness gaps: no GET /comments/:id is tested for the missing-comment 404 case, and there is no validation that assigneeId or userId actually exist as users in TaskService/ProjectService (cross-service validation is deferred to the router only for comments, inconsistently). Code quality is high: idiomatic TypeScript, proper use of Map stores, immutable updates via spread, typed payloads on the event bus, and solid error handling in the router. The main code quality issue is the use of require('http') inside the demo's request() helper — a CommonJS dynamic require inside an ESM/tsx file is an antipattern and should be a top-level import. Constraint compliance deductions: (1) the demo.ts uses require() instead of an import, violating the no-external-pattern spirit and ESM consistency; (2) the router reads from both taskSvc and userSvc to resolve context before calling commentSvc.create() — this is explicitly justified in a comment as a router-layer concern and is architecturally defensible, but it does mean the router has read-coupling to two services to serve a third, which is a mild boundary smell; (3) the eventBus singleton is a module-level global shared across all service instances, which works but makes test isolation difficult and is not flagged as a concern. No external npm dependencies are used in application code. Each service is in its own file. The forward-only transition table is correctly implemented. All six architectural rules are substantially respected.
